mcqs.question: A reviewer leaves a two-word comment on your PR: "this won't scale." What is the most productive way to read and answer it?
options: Reply asking them to rewrite the comment in a more constructive tone before you engage with it
Treat the brevity as a signal they don't respect the change and request a different reviewer
Make the change they seem to want, since arguing with a senior reviewer rarely goes well
Read it as a request for the scaling argument, and reply with the numbers: expected volume, what the hot path costs, where it would break
mcqs.explanation: Terse usually means rushed, not hostile — reading it charitably turns a two-word verdict into an answerable technical question, and supplying the volume and cost data lets the reviewer either concede or point at the case you missed. Demanding a tone rewrite stalls the PR over the wrapper instead of the substance, and silently complying hides whether the concern was even real.

mcqs.question: A reviewer asks you to add a mutex around an initialization path you believe is single-threaded. Which reply is the strongest pushback?
options: "This path only runs during startup, before the HTTP listener binds, so no concurrent caller exists yet — the lock would add contention with no correctness benefit. Is there a call site I'm missing?"
"I've worked on this service for two years and it has never had a race here."
"I don't think that's right, but I'll add it if you insist."
"Adding a mutex here would hurt performance."
mcqs.explanation: Strong pushback names the specific mechanism — when the code runs relative to concurrency being possible — so the reviewer can verify it or point at the exception, and the closing question keeps it collaborative rather than final. Tenure, vague disagreement, and an unquantified performance claim all give the reviewer nothing to check, so the thread needs another round just to locate the real disagreement.

mcqs.question: You argued for approach A, the tech lead decided on B, and you're implementing B. Which behavior violates disagree-and-commit?
options: Writing a short comment recording that you preferred A and why, then implementing B fully
Asking for a revisit six months later when B has produced concrete, measurable problems
Implementing B but leaving out the error handling it needs, and adding a TODO noting this is why A was better
Telling a teammate privately that you still think A was the better call
mcqs.explanation: Half-implementing the decision so it underperforms is sabotage even when it's unintentional — the whole point of committing is that the chosen approach gets a fair execution. Recording your position, holding a private opinion, and revisiting later on new evidence are all compatible with committing; what isn't compatible is letting the disagreement leak into the quality of the work.

mcqs.question: You and a reviewer are on the third round of the same comment thread and neither position has moved. What's the best next step?
options: Keep writing in the thread but with more detail each round, since the written record is valuable
Approve the reviewer's version to unblock the PR and raise the concern in a later refactor
Move it to a short call, then post a one-line summary of the outcome back on the PR
Escalate straight to a tech lead, since three rounds proves you're deadlocked
mcqs.explanation: Three rounds with no movement means text is losing the nuance, and a five-minute call usually resolves it — but the outcome has to land back on the PR or the decision is invisible to everyone who wasn't on the call. Escalating first skips the cheaper step, and longer comments repeat the failing medium rather than changing it.

mcqs.question: Why is silently implementing a review comment you believe is wrong worse for the team than arguing about it?
options: The disagreement stays unresolved and resurfaces later with resentment attached, and authors start routing reviews away from that reviewer
It slows the PR down more than a comment thread would
It signals to the reviewer that their comment was low quality
It leaves the codebase in an inconsistent state that a linter can't catch
mcqs.explanation: Silent compliance looks like a clean merge, so nothing gets corrected — the same argument returns in the next PR, and the quiet workaround of requesting review from someone less likely to push back degrades review quality across the team. It's actually the fastest option for that single PR, which is exactly why it's tempting and why the cost is invisible.

mcqs.question: Which review comment is most worth spending a long disagreement thread on?
options: A reviewer preferring a guard clause where you wrote an if/else, with identical behavior
A request to rename a private helper from `parseRow` to `rowToRecord`
A suggested extraction of two lines into a named function, which you find slightly less readable
A requested retry-on-failure that would make a non-idempotent payment call run twice
mcqs.explanation: Retrying a non-idempotent payment is a correctness bug with money attached — that's a hill worth taking, and worth escalating if it doesn't resolve. The other three are stylistic preferences with no meaningful difference in correctness, maintainability or performance, where the cost of arguing exceeds the cost of just making the change.
